exam: A 28‑year‑old at 30 weeks presents with preterm labour contractions – what is your next step? — Give a full course of ACS immediately, then assess need for tocolysis.
How does ACS reduce intraventricular haemorrhage? — By stabilising cerebral vasculature through reduced fluctuations in blood flow and improving platelet function.
A woman with well‑controlled type 1 diabetes is in preterm labour – do you give ACS? — Yes, after checking glucose; treat any hyperglycaemia but do not withhold ACS.
What is the contraindication to ACS in a woman with suspected infection? — Active chorioamnionitis (maternal fever, uterine tenderness, foul amniotic fluid).
Explain why a repeat dose of ACS is not given routinely. — Benefit wanes after 7 days and repeated exposure raises risk of fetal growth restriction and maternal infection.
In a low‑resource setting without surfactant, why is ACS especially important? — It reduces the incidence and severity of RDS, decreasing the need for mechanical ventilation that may be unavailable.
Differentiate ACS from tocolytic therapy in preterm labour. — ACS matures fetal lungs; tocolytics aim to delay delivery without affecting lung maturity.
If a woman receives only one dose of betamethasone before emergency Caesarean, what should you do? — Complete the second dose as soon as possible, even post‑delivery, to confer neonatal benefit.
ai.title: Antenatal Corticosteroids
ai.subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
ai.summary: Antenatal corticosteroids accelerate fetal lung maturation and reduce neonatal morbidity when preterm birth is imminent. Use is guided by gestational age, timing, and maternal condition, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Key gestational window: 24 + 0 to 34 + 6 weeks
Optimal benefit when birth occurs 24 h–7 days after the first dose
sections.p: Antenatal corticosteroids (ACS) are given to women at risk of preterm delivery (24‑34 weeks) to stimulate surfactant production and improve lung compliance in the fetus.

t.b: Confirms eligibility; if ultrasound unavailable, use last menstrual period with caution
Identifies contraindication (active chorioamnionitis); if labs unavailable, rely on clinical signs

b: Surfactant synthesis peaks after 48 h of exposure
Effect wanes after 7 days – repeat course only if risk persists
Benefit outweighs potential maternal hyperglycaemia in most cases
sections.p: Corticosteroids cross the placenta and up‑regulate type II pneumocyte surfactant proteins, reducing respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) and intraventricular hemorrhage.

b: Reduces RDS incidence by ~50 %
Lowers neonatal mortality by 30‑40 % in settings without surfactant therapy
May reduce need for mechanical ventilation, preserving scarce equipment
sections.p: In low‑resource hospitals, ACS is often the only intervention to improve outcomes for preterm infants where neonatal ventilation is limited.

t.b: Determines whether to give ACS now or wait; if delivery is certain within 24 h, give full course immediately
Monitor blood glucose; treat hyperglycaemia if severe, but do not withhold ACS

b: Indication: imminent preterm birth <34 weeks, regardless of mode of delivery
Contraindication: maternal systemic infection not controlled, or fetal demise
Repeat dose: only if >7 days have passed and risk persists
sections.p: Examiners test understanding of indications, timing, contraindications, and interpretation of outcomes.

Limited investigations are needed; focus on clinical assessment.
